title: Trustworthy AI
description: You learn to connect specific failure paths to controls and release decisions.

readerInvitation.reasonToExist: This engineering course asks what evidence justifies relying on each new capability.
readerInvitation.readerPromise: You learn to connect specific failure paths to controls and release decisions.
readerOutcomes: Identify a bounded reliance claim and the system it concerns.
Distinguish source availability from support validation and choose the stated grounded-task fallback.
Recognize evidence affected by a repository change despite unchanged generator weights.
Ask what evidence could change a release decision.

readerInvitation.audienceFit: Readers interested in the book's central problem who want to examine its distinctions, evidence, proposals and limitations before adopting its conclusions.

contentSamples.readingValue: Understand what the selected grounded-policy task should do when its source becomes unavailable.

Connect the technical failure trace to informed organizational authority.

readerInvitation.closingInvitation: Begin with From Model Scores to Justified Reliance, then follow Meridian's expanding responsibilities. Building an Assurance Case brings those lessons together into a reviewable engineering argument.

sources.title: Front matter
ABOUT THIS EDITION
CONTENTS
1. Why Trustworthy AI Is an Engineering Problem
1.1 From Model Scores to Justified Reliance
1.2 Failure Has a Context, a Cost, and a Path to Harm
1.3 Assurance Mindset: Claims, Evidence, and Residual Uncertainty
2. Define the System Before You Measure It
2.1 The Four-Layer System: Data, Model, Harness, Organization
2.2 Lifecycle, Change, and Evidence Decay
2.3 Requirements, Traceability, and the Operating Envelope
3. Reliability in a Changing and Adversarial World
3.1 Distribution Shift: IID Is a Convenience, Not a Law
3.2 Robustness, Adversarial Pressure, and Failure Budgets
3.3 Fault Injection, Recovery, and Graceful Degradation
4. Uncertainty, Calibration, and Safe Decisions
4.1 Accuracy, Confidence, and Calibration
4.2 Abstention, Selective Prediction, and Conformal Guarantees
4.3 Uncertainty in Language Models, Tool Use, and Decisions
5. Explainability, Interpretability, and Causal Understanding
5.1 Explanation for Whom, and for What Decision?
5.2 From Behavioral Explanation to Mechanistic Interpretability
5.3 Testing Explanations and Avoiding Explanation Theater
6. Fairness, Human Impact, and Distributional Harm
6.1 The Measurement Problem: Targets, Labels, and Historical Data
6.2 Conflicting Fairness Criteria, Causality, and Long-Term Effects
6.3 Intersectionality, Shift, and Socio-Technical Validation
7. Privacy and Security as System Properties
7.1 From Training Data to Inference-Time Leakage
7.2 Adversarial ML, Prompt Injection, and the Supply Chain
7.3 Least Privilege, Provenance, and Defense in Depth
8. Verification, Testing, and Evaluation Science
8.1 A Testing Pyramid for AI Systems
8.2 Formal Methods, Verified Harnesses, and Runtime Assurance
8.3 Benchmarks, Contamination, LLM Judges, and External Validity
9. Trustworthy Generative AI
9.1 Hallucination, Factuality, RAG, and Claim-Level Grounding
9.2 Safety Tuning, Refusal, Misuse, and Frontier Risk
9.3 System Cards, Model Updates, and Open Weights
10. Trustworthy Agents and Multi-Agent Systems
10.1 Actions, Tools, Memory, and Authority
10.2 Agent Hijacking, Long Horizons, and Multi-Agent Failure
10.3 Evaluating and Constraining Agents in Practice
11. Humans, Governance, Standards, and Regulation
11.1 Calibrated Reliance, Automation Bias, and the Human-AI Team
11.2 Governance and Standards as Engineering Infrastructure
11.3 The EU AI Act in 2026: Translating Obligations into Technical Work
12. Assurance Engineering and Beyond the State of the Art
12.1 Building an Assurance Case
12.2 Continuous, Executable, and Compositional Assurance
12.3 Beyond 2026: Mechanistic Assurance, Evaluation-Resistant
CLOSING SYNTHESIS
